opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the most plausible near-term path doesn't look like the classic sci-fi picture of a model rewriting its own weights in some dramatic way. It's much more mundane, and that's partly what makes it worth taking seriously.

The basic idea is that AI research is itself largely a software engineering and experimentation task. A lot of what researchers at frontier labs actually do day to day is write code, run experiments, debug training runs, look at results, tweak hyperparameters, and try again. Those are exactly the kinds of tasks where we've seen models improve really quickly. So the question becomes: at what point are models good enough at that work to meaningfully speed up the people doing it, and then at what point can they do substantial chunks of it on their own?

One way we've tried to get a handle on this is by measuring the length of tasks models can complete autonomously, roughly how long a task would take a skilled human. That horizon has been growing fast, doubling on the order of every several months. If you extrapolate, even with a lot of uncertainty, you get to models that can reliably do tasks that take a human days or weeks within a few years. At that point you're talking about real research projects, not just snippets of code.

Then you get the feedback loop. If AI systems are doing a meaningful fraction of AI R&D, progress speeds up, which produces more capable systems, which speed things up further. And labs have strong incentives to do this. They're compute-constrained and talent-constrained, and if you can run thousands of copies of a model that's as good as a decent research engineer, that's an enormous multiplier.

I want to be careful about uncertainty, though. There are real bottlenecks. Compute doesn't scale instantly just because your researchers got faster. Some research taste and judgment may be harder to automate than raw engineering. And benchmark performance doesn't always translate cleanly into real-world usefulness. Messy, underspecified, long-horizon work is where models still struggle most.

But I don't think we can confidently rule it out on a short timescale, and that's the part I care about. If this happens, it might happen inside a lab, fairly quietly, before the outside world has good visibility into it. So a big part of what I think matters is building the measurement infrastructure now: evaluations that track AI R&D capability specifically, transparency from developers about how much they're using their own models internally, and agreed-upon thresholds where, if you see these capabilities, you need much stronger safety and security measures in place. You really don't want to be figuring out how to measure this after it's already underway.

r005.rationale: It does not raise the possibility that poor elicitation conceals superhuman prediction of experimental outcomes.

r006.rationale: It does not suggest using accurate predictions to replace experiments and accelerate research.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that recursive self-improvement probably doesn't look like one dramatic moment where a model rewrites its own weights and takes off. The near-term version is much more mundane, and honestly that's what makes it plausible. It looks like AI systems doing an increasing fraction of the actual labor of AI R&D.

So think about what a research engineer at a frontier lab actually does day to day. They write training code, they debug distributed systems, they design experiments, they run ablations, they look at the results and decide what to try next. A lot of that is already being partially automated. Models are writing a large share of the code at these labs. And the question is just, how much of the loop can you close? If you get to the point where a model can take a vaguely specified research direction, implement it, run the experiment, interpret the results, and propose the next experiment, with humans mostly just reviewing, then you've got a very fast feedback loop, because the thing being improved is the thing doing the improving.

At METR we've been trying to measure this fairly directly. We look at how long the tasks are, in terms of how long they'd take a human expert, that models can complete autonomously with reasonable reliability. And that horizon has been doubling roughly every several months. If you extrapolate that even a couple of years, you're at tasks that take skilled humans days or weeks. That's the regime where you can hand off meaningful chunks of research.

The thing I'd caution against is thinking this requires some conceptual breakthrough in the models. It mostly requires reliability, and it requires the labs to actually build the scaffolding and give the systems the compute and permissions to run experiments. Those are engineering and organizational choices, not deep scientific ones, which is partly why I think the timeline could be short.

The other piece is that the bottleneck shifts. Once you have automated researchers, your constraint becomes compute for experiments rather than human hours, and that changes the dynamics. You might see a lot of progress on algorithmic efficiency specifically, because that's what you'd point a bunch of tireless automated researchers at when GPUs are the scarce thing.

What worries me about this is less that it happens and more that we're not well positioned to notice when it's happening, or to know whether the systems doing the work are trustworthy. If a model is running thousands of experiments and summarizing results for you, you're very dependent on it being honest and on you having good evals for the things you actually care about. That's where I think the measurement and oversight work has to keep pace, and right now I'm not confident it is.

astra-6.text:
I think the most plausible route is AI systems getting good enough at AI research that they can substantially accelerate the process of building the next generation. You don’t necessarily need a system that can inspect its own weights and rewrite itself. It could be doing fairly familiar research work: writing code, running experiments, interpreting results, and proposing improvements to training methods.

Initially, humans might still be choosing the research directions and checking the results. But if the AI can take on more of that work, you get a feedback loop: better AI makes research faster, and faster research produces better AI.

The big uncertainty is how strong that feedback loop is. If progress depends mainly on ideas and software experiments that can be done quickly, it could move quite fast. If you’re waiting for a huge training run or more hardware, that puts limits on the speed. So I’d look less for a dramatic moment when an AI suddenly starts modifying itself, and more for the point where AI systems are doing a substantial fraction of the work that improves AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most plausible route is that you get AI systems that are good enough to substantially automate AI research. You don’t necessarily need a system that can rewrite its own code and immediately become smarter. It could be doing the things human researchers currently do: coming up with experiments, writing the code, interpreting the results, and suggesting what to try next.

Then you have a feedback loop where better AI systems help you build better AI systems, which can do more of that research. The important question is how much that speeds things up. If you’re still waiting on long training runs or new hardware, those are bottlenecks. But if a lot of progress comes from finding better algorithms or using existing compute more efficiently, the loop could potentially become quite fast.

So I’d look less for a dramatic moment where a model starts modifying itself, and more for the point where AI is doing a substantial fraction of the work that produces the next generation.
